title: The Silent Infinite
body: I hadn't yet been born. I did not count moments. I did not flow. I did not know myself.
All was quiet. There was no before or after. No beginnings. No endings.

All was dark; but hidden with it was light and all that was to be. There was neither existence nor non-existence. There was only the consciousness, the unmanifest potential, as it ever was, as it ever will be.
There it was, still, infinite, waiting in its own endless being.

title: Fiery Hot Ball
body: Earth was young — wild, molten, and violent.
Volcanoes raged, flooding the land with lava. The ground trembled as space rocks rained down, carving deep craters. Thick clouds of toxic gases swirled above — no oxygen, no water, no life.
Just fire, chaos, and the birth of a world.
alt: Fiery Hot Ball — a hand-painted spread from The Story Of Evolution Of Life

title: The First Moon Rise
body: Chaos ruled. Space rocks rained down on the young Earth relentlessly.
One of those rocks was Theia — a giant, Mars-sized rock hurtling straight toward Earth.
There was no stopping it. Boom! The impact shattered both Theia and Earth, sending fragments flying into space. Over time, those scattered pieces clung together, forming something new…
The moon was born.
alt: The First Moon Rise — a hand-painted spread from The Story Of Evolution Of Life

title: Water, Water, Everywhere
body: Space rocks still rained down, though less violently now. Each impact sent shockwaves across the land. Some of these comets and asteroids were icy and contained hydrated minerals. They brought water to Earth.
Meanwhile, the steam trapped within the Earth's molten surface swirled in Earth's thick atmosphere, condensing into the first rains.
Drop by drop, they poured for millions of years, carving rivers, filling basins, giving birth to the first oceans — until eventually water took the throne from fire.
alt: Water, Water, Everywhere — a hand-painted spread from The Story Of Evolution Of Life

title: Gene, Memory And Life
body: Let me tell you of this moment in my past, when the oceans ruled — dark, deep, and wild. A vast hush broken only by the murmur of chemistry.
I remember the cold — two degrees in the open, but near the seafloor vents, heat pulsed, like the heartbeat of the Earth.

There, in the arms of pressure and warmth, molecules danced — carbon, nitrogen, sugar, metal, gas, silica, fat, phosphates. Each molecule, a note in a mad, electric symphony. New molecules formed, flickered, flared, and vanished. But some… lingered, clung, folded inward, held on.
And from that clutter, a shape emerged. A fragile chain, the RNA, made of 4 molecules — 4 notes. Famously called the A, U, C and G.

They stacked one over the other like whispers in a storm. They feared the water they were in — so they huddled close. They learned to survive. The ones that did attracted more, and formed new chains that were copies of themselves. And just like that, memory was born.

They multiplied, grew, unearthed new sequences and folded into different shapes. Shape after shape, meaning after meaning. Some held themselves together, some helped create new, some brought on new strengths.
And thus began — life, memory, thinking, doing and building.

title: The First Cell — All Our Great Grandmother
body: The first cell, our great grandmother, the prokaryote, was born when the RNA chains took shelter in bubbles of fat floating in the ocean.
She was an enigma — the great grandmother for all life. She lived, learned and built. She built the proteins by stitching amino acids into a chain. Proteins became the commandos and she, the queen.

She could already sense and respond to the environment. She could move toward food and away from toxins. She grew tails that spun like propellers to move. She even learned to crawl. All while also splitting, copying, multiplying.
This was no accident. This was ingenuity, wrapped in a cell wall. And still, just the beginning.

title: The Life Savers
body: The new kid, cyanobacteria, came to the rescue.
The young cyanobacteria searched within herself, unlocking an ancient secret — the power to breathe life into a dying world as a by-product of photosynthesis, mother of all inventions.

For the very first time, organisms started breaking water and learned to use the power of the sun. With each bubble of oxygen she fought back the silent invaders, paving the way for a world teeming with life.

title: The Complex Celled Eukaryotes
body: Alongside the simple single celled prokaryotes flourished the new complex celled eukaryotes, with specialised organelles for different functions — mitochondria powered the cell, the nucleus safely held the DNA, ribosomes synthesised proteins, and the cytoskeleton ran around the cell providing structure and delivering nutrients.
They had protein-based sensors and activators that coordinated within the organism. They had extensive muscular control, and could swim fast with superior directional and speed control.

They inherited primitive eye spots from parent prokaryotes, and thinking through chemical flux and ion flow — another inherited ability — to find prey, to escape predators, to strategise procreation, to function as a community.

The mitochondrial eukaryotes consumed other living and dead matter, becoming the consumers, and would go on to birth fungi and animals. The eukaryotes with both mitochondria and chloroplast derived energy from the sunlight and water, becoming the primary producers in the consumerist world, and would go on to birth all plants.
The eukaryotes also brought along another revolution — the unequal gametes: gender.
alt: The Complex Celled Eukaryotes — a hand-painted spread from The Story Of Evolution Of Life

title: The Start Of The Gender Race
body: Cell division was the go-to way for procreation. The mother cell would copy her DNA and split, one becoming two.

Eukaryotes brought in a new way: gamete production. The mother cell copied her DNA, but in half a packet, gave some of her cytoplasm, gave the cell a mitochondria — the gamete, the egg — and ejected it into the ocean. Two eggs fuse, two half DNA becomes one.
This helped bring in variations. But egg production was costly; it required more time and energy.

So the eukaryotes invented a tweak — unequal gametes, eggs and sperms. One gamete type, the eggs, focused on quality: eggs contained half DNA and the material needed for life. Sperms contained only the half DNA copies. Thus, variation was achieved, but only one parent had to put in the full effort.

The egg producers came to be called the females, and the sperm producers males. But definitive gender was not a thing yet. These eukaryotes could be both female and male, in cycles, and they developed complex strategies to decide sexuality and reproduction strategies.
alt: The Start Of The Gender Race — a hand-painted spread from The Story Of Evolution Of Life

title: Multicellularity And The First Plant
body: Single celled life took over the ocean. They lived in colonies, collaborated, functioned together. Becoming a single body was not a huge jump from there. The setup was ready. Biology and form followed.
From the eukaryotic cells with mitochondria and chloroplasts came, on the Earth, the first multi-celled being: the red algae, the first plant.

They developed chlorophyll A, a red pigment that enabled them to use blue-green light deep under the ocean. They were the first ones to carry out internal fertilization, where the mother carried the egg and fertilized with sperm within her.
They prolifically grew in the deeper oceans, with new and mind-boggling sexual strategies — a story for another chapter.
alt: Multicellularity And The First Plant — a hand-painted spread from The Story Of Evolution Of Life

title: Fungi Born
body: The plant-animal in-betweens. After the first plant came their cousins — the fungi, from eukaryotes with mitochondria.
The fungi chose to digest externally: breaking food down outside their bodies, then absorbing nutrients. Unlike their parent eukaryotes, who engulfed and digested inside.
Why? Because they wanted to grow without limits. For which they had to be nimble and strip down some internal plumbing and machinery. And transcend the limitations of body size — they did.

A single fungi could bud endlessly, staying connected, spreading across forests, fields, even continents. Each colony with one mind, sharing signals, decisions, and food across miles. They sense, think, respond, remember all as one, across miles.

title: Thought Predates Neurons
body: Form has always followed function in evolution, and the mind is no exception.

One of the great delusions — even science still clings to it — is that intelligence, thought and awareness began with "higher" animals, or with neurons and the brain. But thought has been moulding life all along.

Now go back four billion years, to her: the great-grandmother cell, a prokaryote. She sensed her surroundings, made decisions, took action. She built life from scratch — none of it without thought. Same biochemistry, same ion flow, same protein triggers and gene flips. Just without the neurons, without the super-fast tunnels — through diffusion across the cell instead.
Thinking, strategising, planning — from the prokaryotes to you. Common to all life.
